reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A localised disease of the bony labyrinth in which normal bone is replaced by spongy, vascular new bone that most often fixes the stapes footplate
Typically presents in young to middle-aged adults with slowly progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss and a family history
Often worsens during pregnancy, suggesting a hormonal influence, and is more common in women
Patients frequently hear better in noisy surroundings (paracusis Willisii) and may speak softly
The tympanic membrane is characteristically normal; a pink flush over the promontory (Schwartze sign) reflects active vascular disease
Tuning fork tests show a negative Rinne and audiometry reveals conductive loss, often with the characteristic Carhart notch dip in bone conduction around 2 kHz
Cochlear otosclerosis can add a sensorineural component leading to mixed hearing loss
Management options include a hearing aid, or stapes surgery (stapedectomy/stapedotomy with a prosthesis) to restore ossicular movement; sodium fluoride may be used to stabilise active disease
reference.pathophysiology: Otosclerosis is a primary disorder of endochondral bone of the otic capsule in which foci of normal lamellar bone are resorbed and replaced by irregular, highly cellular and vascular spongy bone that later matures into dense sclerotic bone. The commonest site is the region of the fissula ante fenestram just anterior to the oval window; as the focus enlarges it invades and fixes the stapes footplate, producing progressive conductive hearing loss. Extension of foci into the cochlear endosteum can damage the neural elements and cause sensorineural loss. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, and hormonal factors appear to modulate its activity.
additionalDifferentials: Ossicular fixation or discontinuity from other causes
Van der Hoeve syndrome (otosclerosis with osteogenesis imperfecta)
Paget disease of the temporal bone
Superior semicircular canal dehiscence mimicking conductive loss
additionalInvestigations: Pure tone audiometry to document conductive or mixed loss and the Carhart notch
Tuning fork tests to confirm conductive hearing loss
Tympanometry, typically showing normal to reduced compliance, with absent stapedial reflexes
Speech audiometry to assess discrimination before surgery
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to map active foci and exclude other pathology in selected cases
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or asymmetrical sensorineural loss prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Vertigo or disequilibrium suggesting labyrinthine or alternative pathology
Sudden deterioration or facial nerve symptoms after stapes surgery requiring urgent review
Unilateral pulsatile tinnitus or other features that raise concern for a vascular or retrocochlear lesion
reference.prognosis: The disease is progressive but stapes surgery closes the conductive gap and restores useful hearing in most suitably selected patients, while hearing aids remain an effective non-surgical option; established cochlear involvement, however, is not reversible.
pitfalls: Overlooking otosclerosis when the drum looks normal and attributing the loss to wax or effusion
Failing to counsel about the small risk of dead ear and sensorineural loss with stapes surgery
Missing a coexisting sensorineural (cochlear) component that limits surgical benefit
Not recognising the Carhart notch as a bone conduction artefact rather than true cochlear loss
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Stapes surgery, stapedotomy or stapedectomy, to close the conductive gap by bypassing the fixed stapes footplate in suitably selected patients
Hearing aids as an effective non-surgical alternative for those unfit for or declining surgery
Pure-tone and speech audiometry to select surgical candidates and document the conductive or mixed loss
Cochlear implantation for advanced cochlear (retrofenestral) otosclerosis with profound sensorineural loss
Consider sodium fluoride or a bisphosphonate to stabilise active otospongiotic foci in selected cochlear disease
Counsel that established sensorineural cochlear involvement is not reversible by surgery
